# Breadth-First Traversal

## Summary

Given a graph and a starting node, visit every reachable node in breadth-first
order — the start, then all of its neighbours, then everything one step further
out — and return the visit order.

## Constraints

- The graph is undirected in most cases, but the algorithm does not care.
- Nodes unreachable from the start are not visited.
- Cycles and self-loops must not cause a node to be visited twice.
- Neighbours are explored in the order they appear in the adjacency list, so the
  output order is deterministic.

## How the test cases are encoded

`tests/bfs-traversal.json` stores the graph as an adjacency list indexed by node
id: `graph[i]` holds the neighbours of node `i`, so ids are `0..n-1`. Each input
is `[graph, start]`. (The Python starter uses a dictionary instead; either works
— convert when you read the case.)

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[[1,2],[0,3],[0,3],[1,2]], 0` | `[0, 1, 2, 3]` | ring visited level by level |
| `[[1,2],[0,3],[0,3],[1,2]], 3` | `[3, 1, 2, 0]` | the start node decides the order |
| `[[1],[0],[3],[2]], 0` | `[0, 1]` | the second component is never reached |
| `[[0,1],[0]], 0` | `[0, 1]` | a self-loop is visited once |

## Edge Cases

- A single node with no edges.
- A disconnected graph — BFS from one component returns only that component.
- Self-loops and cycles, which loop forever without a visited set.
- Starting from a leaf rather than a hub.
- A node reachable by two different paths, which must not be queued twice.

## Complexity

- **Time:** `O(V + E)` — every node is dequeued once and every edge inspected
  once (twice for an undirected graph, once from each end).
- **Space:** `O(V)` for the queue plus the visited set.

## Why This Category

BFS is one of the two ways to walk a graph, and the one that gives shortest
paths in an unweighted graph for free: the first time a node is dequeued, it is
at minimum edge distance from the start. That property is why BFS underlies
word ladders, grid shortest paths, and level-order tree traversal — a tree being
just a graph with no cycles.

## Thought Process

- Mark nodes visited **when they are enqueued**, not when they are dequeued.
  Marking on dequeue lets the same node enter the queue several times through
  different neighbours, and the traversal degrades badly on dense graphs.
- The queue must be a real queue. Using a list and `pop(0)` in Python is `O(n)`
  per removal — `collections.deque` exists for this.
- Swap the queue for a stack and you have DFS; the difference between the two
  algorithms is one data structure.
- To get shortest *distances* rather than an order, store `(node, depth)` pairs
  or process the queue one full level at a time.
